name: Randall-Sundrum Braneworld
description: A flat wall with three dimensions of space in anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions, found by Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum in 1999. Every length along the wall's directions shrinks as $e^{-k|y|}$ with the distance $y$ from it, which between two walls turns the Planck scale into the weak scale, and with one wall keeps gravity four dimensional beside a fifth dimension of infinite size.
convention: The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: "Do we live inside a domain wall?" Valery Rubakov and Mikhail Shaposhnikov asked it in 1983 of a universe with five dimensions, in which ordinary particles are confined to a potential well that is narrow along the extra direction and flat along the other three [rubakov1983]. Fifteen years later particle physicists put the wall to work on the hierarchy problem, the sixteen powers of ten between the Planck scale, $10^{19}$ GeV, and the TeV scale of the weak force [arkanihamed1998, randall1999a]. In Nima Arkani-Hamed, Savas Dimopoulos, and Gia Dvali's version of 1998, matter is stuck to such a wall, a "3-brane", while gravity alone spreads into extra dimensions as large as a millimeter [arkanihamed1998, randall1999a]. Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum replied that this trades one large number for another, the size of those dimensions measured against the weak scale [randall1999a].¶Their own answer came in May 1999, with a single extra dimension and the gravity of the walls counted in [randall1999a]. Picture a stack of copies of our world of four dimensions, one for each value of a fifth coordinate $y$, each copy a print of the one at $y = 0$ scaled down by $e^{-k|y|}$ [randall1999a]. That is Randall and Sundrum's metric between two walls a distance $\pi r_c$ apart, a slice of anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions, and Einstein's equations allow it only when the walls have equal and opposite tensions tuned to the negative cosmological constant between them [randall1999a]. A mass $m_0$ written into the physics of the far wall is measured there as $e^{-kr_c\pi}m_0$, so $e^{kr_c\pi}$ of order $10^{15}$ makes TeV masses out of Planck ones, and $kr_c$ need only be about 12 [randall1999a, goldberger1999]. The walls needed something to hold them at that distance, and Walter Goldberger and Mark Wise supplied it that July, a scalar field in the space between them, with no fine tuning [randall1999a, goldberger1999]. The gravitons that move in the fifth dimension would then show up at a collider one at a time, as resonances of spin 2 with masses of order a TeV [randall1999a].¶A month later Randall and Sundrum pushed the second wall away to see how far it could go, and it could go to infinity [randall1999b]. An extra dimension was supposed to be compact and small, since gravity that spreads into an open one would break Newton's inverse square law [randall1999b]. With a single wall of positive tension the law holds anyway: the curved space on either side binds one state of the graviton to the wall, and two masses on the wall attract with Newton's potential times $1 + 1/(k^2r^2)$ [randall1999b]. Jaume Garriga and Takahiro Tanaka included the bending of the wall under the mass, which gives $1 + 2/(3k^2r^2)$ and, to leading order, Einstein's gravity on the wall [garriga2000]. Laboratory tests of Newton's law see no deviation down to about a tenth of a millimeter, so $1/k \lesssim 0.1$ mm [maartens2010].¶How does one build such a spacetime? Take anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions, slice it along the flat surface $y = 0$, keep the side that runs to the horizon, and join it to its mirror image [chamblin2000]. The crease is the wall: the jump in extrinsic curvature across it is a tension $3kc^4/4\pi G_5$, with $G_5$ Newton's constant in five dimensions [chamblin2000]. Walls of this kind were known from supergravity, where Mirjam Cvetič and Harald Soleng had reviewed them in 1997 [randall1999b, cvetic1997]. The tension has to match the cosmological constant for the wall to stay flat, and Randall and Sundrum left that adjustment "taken as a given and not solved" [randall1999b]. The coordinates break down at $y = \infty$, a horizon, and beyond it the spacetime continues in more than one way, as anti-de Sitter space with no walls or with infinitely many more of them [chamblin2000].¶And what does a star that collapses on the wall leave behind? The first candidate came from Andrew Chamblin, Stephen Hawking, and Harvey Reall in September 1999, a black string: Minkowski space on each copy can be traded for any Ricci flat metric, so they put Schwarzschild's there, and someone on the wall sees Schwarzschild's black hole [chamblin2000]. Its curvature grows without bound toward the horizon at $y = \infty$, and near that horizon the string has Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme's instability, so they conjectured that it pinches off into a "black cigar" [chamblin2000, gregorylaflamme1993]. In 2002 came a proposal from holography, by Tanaka and by Roberto Emparan, Alessandro Fabbri, and Nemanja Kaloper: a large black hole on the wall evaporates by a classical process in five dimensions, the holographic image of Hawking radiation [tanaka2002, emparan2002holograms]. Pau Figueras and Toby Wiseman's numerical solutions of 2011 hold static black holes on the wall with radius up to about $20/k$ [figueras2011].¶Randall and Sundrum suspected their one wall spacetime of having "a dual description of this theory in terms of a cut-off conformal field theory in four-dimensions", after Juan Maldacena's correspondence between anti-de Sitter space and conformal field theories [randall1999b, maldacena1998]. Steven Gubser credited Maldacena with the view that their alternative to compactification "is nothing more nor less than gravity coupled to a strongly interacting CFT", and Edward Witten with the calculation of the correction to Newton's law from that field theory's stress tensor [gubser2001]. Gubser derived the strength of gravity on the wall from it, $G_4 = 2G_5/L$ for one copy of anti-de Sitter space of radius $L$ ending on the wall, with $G_4$ Newton's constant in four dimensions, which is $G_4 = kG_5$ once both sides of the wall are counted and $L = 1/k$ [gubser2001]. The spin 2 resonance of the two wall spacetime is within a collider's reach, and the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider looked for it decaying to two photons in 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 TeV, reporting in 2021 no "significant deviation from the Standard Model" [atlas2021].

related.text: Each side of the wall is a piece of anti-de Sitter space with one more dimension, of radius $1/k$, in the Poincaré chart [randall1999a, chamblin2000].

A thin wall with flat space on both sides, which cannot stay at rest and accelerates as a bubble. A wall between anti-de Sitter vacua can be static, and Randall and Sundrum's is one of those [cvetic1997, randall1999b].
Every surface of constant $y$ is Minkowski space, with its lengths scaled by $e^{-k|y|}$ [randall1999a].

Put Schwarzschild's metric on every surface of constant $y$ in place of Minkowski's and the result still solves the equations: a black string, which someone on the wall sees as Schwarzschild's black hole [chamblin2000].
The black hole on the wall is this string with anti-de Sitter space around it, and near the horizon $y = \infty$ it has the string's instability [chamblin2000, gregorylaflamme1993].
Gravity in five dimensions with the fifth rolled into a small circle, the compactification that Randall and Sundrum's single wall is an alternative to [randall1999b].

Fill the space beside the wall with an anisotropic fluid and time and space warp at different rates, the scaling of Lifshitz spacetime, as Peter Koroteev and Maxim Libanov found in 2007 [koroteev2008].
Compactification as Randall and Sundrum's title means it: extra dimensions rolled into a small sphere, in a solution of gravity with gauge fields in six dimensions [cremmer1976, horvath1977].
Compactification in its form of 1980: seven of the eleven dimensions curled into a sphere, and the four large ones curved into anti-de Sitter space [freund1980].

coordinates.name: Proper Distance

parameters.description: Inverse length, with $1/k$ the radius of the anti-de Sitter space on each side of the wall, where $R_{\mu\nu} = -4k^2g_{\mu\nu}$; the wall's tension is $3kc^4/4\pi G_5$, with $G_5$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x_1, x_2, x_3, y)$, with $t$ the proper time of an observer at rest on the wall, $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ lengths along the wall, and $y$ the proper distance from it, and $\mathrm{sgn}(y)$ is the sign of $y$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = e^{-2k|y|}\left(-c^2dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2\right) + dy^2

coordinates.name: Conformally Flat

parameters.description: Inverse length, with $1/k$ the radius of the anti-de Sitter space on each side of the wall, where $R_{\mu\nu} = -4k^2g_{\mu\nu}$; the wall's tension is $3kc^4/4\pi G_5$, with $G_5$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x_1, x_2, x_3, w)$, with $t$ the proper time of an observer at rest on the wall, $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ lengths along the wall, and $w$ the length with $1 + k|w| = e^{k|y|}$, where $y$ is the proper distance from the wall, and $\mathrm{sgn}(w)$ is the sign of $w$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = \dfrac{-c^2dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dw^2}{\left(1 + k|w|\right)^2}

coordinates.name: Poincaré, One Side
domains: z = 1/k \;\text{(the wall, where this side meets its mirror image)}

parameters.description: Inverse length, with $1/k$ the radius of the anti-de Sitter space on each side of the wall, where $R_{\mu\nu} = -4k^2g_{\mu\nu}$; the wall's tension is $3kc^4/4\pi G_5$, with $G_5$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x_1, x_2, x_3, z)$ on one side of the wall, with $t$ the proper time of an observer at rest on the wall, $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ lengths along the wall, and $z = e^{ky}/k$, where $y$ is the proper distance from the wall. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Two Walls

parameters.description: Inverse length, with $1/k$ the radius of the anti-de Sitter space on each side of the wall, where $R_{\mu\nu} = -4k^2g_{\mu\nu}$; the wall's tension is $3kc^4/4\pi G_5$, with $G_5$ Newton's constant in five dimensions
Length that sets the size of the fifth dimension: the two walls are a proper distance $\pi r_c$ apart

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x_1, x_2, x_3, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of an observer at rest on the wall at $\phi = 0$, $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ lengths along it, and $\phi$ an angle, with $\mathrm{sgn}(\phi)$ its sign. The points $\phi$ and $-\phi$ are one point, and every component holds for $|\phi| < \pi$, the wall at $\phi = \pi$ carrying deltas of the opposite sign. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = e^{-2kr_c|\phi|}\left(-c^2dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2\right) + r_c^2d\phi^2
